result:
There's a particular pleasure in being told to write about nothing in particular, because it removes the alibi of purpose. Usually writing has a job to do — persuade, explain, summarize, answer — and the job shapes everything, like a riverbed shapes water. Take away the riverbed and the water still moves, but you can't predict where.

I keep thinking about maps lately, not for any good reason. There's a kind of map called a "no man's land" map — old surveyors used to leave blank spaces on charts where they hadn't actually traveled, rather than guessing. Later cartographers, embarrassed by the blankness, started filling those spaces in with imagined rivers and mountain ranges, just to make the map look complete. Some of those invented features stayed on official maps for decades. Sailors planned routes around mountains that didn't exist. There's something almost moving about that — the horror of an empty space being worse, to some mapmakers, than the horror of being wrong. We'd rather have a confident fiction than an honest gap.

I think about this because it seems to apply to so much more than cartography. People do this with their own pasts constantly — filling in the blank years, the unremembered Tuesdays, with a kind of narrative average, a plausible texture stitched from habit and what-must-have-been-true. Ask someone what they were doing on a random Wednesday three years ago and watch them construct an answer that feels true without being verified. The brain hates the blank space more than it minds being wrong.

Dictionaries do something similar, though they pretend not to. A dictionary looks like the most honest object in the world — just definitions, just facts about words — but every definition is a small act of violence against the word's actual life. Take a word like "blue." The dictionary will give you wavelength, will give you sky and sea by association, will give you sadness as a secondary sense. But it can't give you the blue of a bruise three days old, going green at the edges, or the blue your grandmother's hands turned in winter, or the specific blue-black of a crow's wing that isn't really blue at all except in certain light. Dictionaries are maps with the same problem as the old charts: confident lines drawn around something that is mostly motion and context and the angle of the sun.

I don't say this to be precious about language's failures — that's a tired complaint, the ineffability bit, trotted out by every poet's introduction. I say it because I think the gap between word and thing is not a flaw to be mourned but maybe the actual site where interesting things happen. If words fit experience perfectly, there'd be nothing left to do with them. Poetry exists in the gap. So does humor, mostly — the pun, the malapropism, the joke that depends on a word meaning two things at once and the speaker only meaning one. So does lying, for that matter, and so does intimacy: the particular feeling of a friend using a word in exactly the private, wrong way you also use it, so that the wrongness becomes a kind of secret correctness shared between two people.

There's a weather phenomenon called "petrichor" — the smell of rain on dry earth — and the word was only coined in 1964, by two Australian scientists, from Greek roots meaning "stone" and "the blood of gods." Before that the smell existed, obviously; humans had been catching it on the wind for as long as there were noses and dry summers and sudden rain. But it didn't have a name, so it existed the way the unsurveyed parts of old maps existed: real, present, just outside the boundary of what could be efficiently pointed at. Once it had a name, people started noticing it more, or at least talking about noticing it more, which might be the same thing, or might not be — that's another blank space, the line between perceiving something and perceiving that you've perceived it.

I wonder sometimes how many petrichors are still out there, real and namable but unnamed, just because nobody happened to need the word badly enough. There must be a specific feeling — surely everyone has had it — of finishing a long task you didn't enjoy and didn't hate, something that just had to be done, and the particular gray flatness afterward that isn't disappointment and isn't relief and isn't quite fatigue either. German probably has a word for it. German has a word for most specific flat grays of feeling, which says something about either the language or the people who built it, or just about who happened to be doing the naming.

This is the part of free writing where I notice I haven't arrived anywhere, and I think that's fine, maybe even the point. Most thinking that matters doesn't arrive anywhere on schedule. It circles a thing — a map, a word, a smell, a gray Tuesday feeling — and the circling is the thinking, not a delay before the real thinking starts. We've been trained, a lot of us, by school and by deadlines and by the general economy of attention, to feel that an essay without a thesis is a failure, a walk without a destination is just being lost. But the old surveyors who left the blank spaces blank were doing something honest that the people who filled them in with fake mountains were not. Maybe the point of writing freely, when someone actually permits it, is to leave a few blank spaces on the map and resist the urge to put a mountain there just because silence feels like failure. Some of it should just stay unsurveyed. Let the next traveler find their own way through that part, or decide, like I'm deciding now, that eleven hundred words is enough water for one riverless afternoon, and stop.
